candidate.stem: System A reaches expert-level performance on a dangerous planning task after extensive training on billions of examples (brute-force learning). System B reaches the identical expert-level performance after minimal, highly sample-efficient training. Under the section's behaviorist framing, how should their risk profiles compare?

options.text: They pose equal risk, since what matters for safety is the capability a system now has, not the learning path that produced it.
System A poses less risk than System B, since reaching the capability through brute force suggests a shallower, less generalizable intelligence.
options.provenance: misreads 'forget about internal mental states and focus on observable behavior' plus the adaptability discussion as implying brute-force-acquired capability is less real or less dangerous than efficiently-acquired capability

options.text: System B poses less risk than System A, since efficient learners are inherently more constrained and predictable than brute-force learners.
options.provenance: reverses the same error in the other direction, treating efficient learning itself as a safety property rather than a separate axis the text declines to link to danger

options.text: Whichever system can be said to truly understand the task poses more risk, since genuine understanding is what enables dangerous autonomous action.
options.provenance: misreads the paired Chinese Room / consciousness discussion as meaning genuine understanding, not observable capability, is what makes a system dangerous

candidate.explanation: Risk tracks what a system can do, not the route it took to get there — that is the whole point of setting the learning-path question aside for safety purposes. Distractor 1 revives the pre-chapter intuition that brute-force learning signals something shallower or less real, when the text is explicit that the risks exist either way once the capability is present. Distractor 2 makes the same mistake in the opposite direction, treating efficient learning as evidence of safety rather than as a separate axis entirely. Distractor 3 imports the consciousness debate this section deliberately sets aside — 'true understanding' has little bearing on whether a system can take a dangerous action. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Case Studies)
candidate.takeaway: Safety-relevant risk is set by what a system can do, not by the path — efficient or brute-force — it took to get there.

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who had internalized 'risk tracks capability, not learning path' would state the key before seeing any option.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might default to 'efficient learning = more advanced = safer,' but the paired scenario forces them to notice the text explicitly rejects learning-path as a safety-relevant variable, so that shortcut fails.
